label: 3.7-rmk1
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{3.7-rmk1}
One can show that
$L^\infty_{{\mathbb{F}}}\big(\Omega;L^p(0,T;{\cal L}({\cal X};{\cal Y}))\big)\!\subset\!
\Upsilon_p({\cal X};{\cal Y})$. For any $L(\cdot,\cdot)\!\in
\Upsilon_p({\cal X};{\cal Y})$, one does not need to have
$L(\cdot,\cdot)\in
L^\infty_{{\mathbb{F}}}\big(\Omega;L^p(0,T;{\cal L}({\cal X};{\cal Y}))\big)$.
The reason for introducing such set is the lack
of measurability for operator-valued functions
and processes appeared in concrete problems. For
example, generally speaking, a $C_0$-semigroup
is not measurable with respect to the time
variable (e.g.,\cite[Subsection
1.1.c]{Hytonen-et-al-2016}). In such case, one
has to relax the condition on the measurability
of such functions and processes. Nevertheless,
as we shall see later, in some sense
$\Upsilon_p({\cal X}; {\cal Y})$ is a nice ``replacement"
of the space
$L^\infty_{{\mathbb{F}}}\big(\Omega;L^p(0,T;{\cal L}({\cal X};{\cal Y}))\big)$
in the study of stochastic LQ problems.
head: environment

label: 3.7-rmk1-1
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{3.7-rmk1-1}
    ({\bf AS0}) is not restrictive in the sense that, as far as we know, all the linear SPDEs satisfies it.

label: 3.7-rmk1-2
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{3.7-rmk1-2}
    ({\bf AS1}) is not restrictive in the sense that, many important SPDEs, such as stochastic wave equations, stochastic heat equations and stochastic Schr\"odinger equations, involved on bounded domains fulfill it..

title: Remark
body_md:
Note the set $H'_\lambda$ depends on the
parameter $\lambda$. Once a
$\lambda=\{\lambda_j\}_{j=1}^\infty\in \ell^2_+$   is
given, we get an $H_\lambda'$, namely,   $H_\lambda'$
depends on the choice of $\lambda$.  Generally
speaking, for two different $\lambda,\hat \lambda\in
\ell^2_+$, the corresponding spaces $H_\lambda'$ and
$H_{\hat\lambda}'$ are different.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In Assumption {\bf (AS3)}, we assume
the existence of one $\lambda\in \ell^2_+$
so that \eqref{3.8-eq1} holds.
Nevertheless, there may exist another
$\hat \lambda \in \ell^2_+$ such that
\eqref{3.8-eq1} does not hold when $\lambda$
is replaced by $\hat \lambda$. Fortunately,
this will not influence the main
results of this paper. In other words,
we only need the existence of one
$\lambda\in \ell^2_+$ such that
\eqref{3.8-eq1} holds to prove our main
results.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For an LQ problem of a given  SPDE,
Assumption {\bf (AS3)} means that some
coefficients in the equation and the
cost functional are smooth in some
sense (See Section \ref{sec-example} for example). This is not very restrictive
for many controlled SPDEs.

label: 4.8-def2
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{4.8-def2}
We call $\big(P(\cdot),\Lambda(\cdot)\big)\in
C_{{\mathbb{F}},w}\big([0,T];
L^{\infty}(\Omega;{\cal S}(H))\big) \times
L^2_{{\mathbb{F}},D,w}(0,T;{\cal S}(H))$ a
transposition solution to
\eqref{5.5-eq6} if the following
 conditions hold:

\medskip

{\rm 1)}  $K(t,\omega)\big(\equiv R(t,\omega) +
D(t,\omega)^*P(t,\omega)D(t,\omega)\big)> 0$ and its left
inverse $K(t,\omega)^{-1}$ is a densely defined
closed operator for a.e. $(t,\omega)\in
[0,T]\times\Omega$;

\medskip

{\rm 2)}  For any $t\in [0,T]$,
$\xi_1,\xi_2\in L^4_{{\cal F}_t}(\Omega;H)$,
$u_1(\cdot), u_2(\cdot)\in
L^4_{\mathbb{F}}(\Omega;L^2(t,T;H))$ and
$v_1(\cdot), v_2(\cdot)$ $\in
L^4_{\mathbb{F}}(\Omega;L^2(t,T;H_\lambda))$, with
$L\=D^* PC+B^*P+D^*\Lambda,$ it holds that
 
\begin{eqnarray}\label{6.18-eq1}
&& \3n\3n\3n {\mathbb{E}}\langle
Gx_{1}(T),x_{2}(T)\rangle_{H} \!+{\mathbb{E}}
\!\int_t^T\!\! \big\langle Q(\tau) x_{1}(\tau),
x_{2}(\tau) \big\rangle_{H}d\tau \!- {\mathbb{E}}
\!\int_t^T\!\! \big\langle K(\tau)^{-1} L(\tau)
x_{1}(\tau), L(\tau)x_{2}(\tau)
\big\rangle_{H}d\tau\nonumber
\\
&&\3n\3n\3n = {\mathbb{E}}\big\langle P(t)
\xi_{1},\xi_{2} \big\rangle_{H} + {\mathbb{E}} \int_t^T
\big\langle P(\tau)u_{1}(\tau),
x_{2}(\tau)\big\rangle_{H}d\tau + {\mathbb{E}} \int_t^T
\big\langle P(\tau)x_{1}(\tau),
u_{2}(\tau)\big\rangle_{H}d\tau \\
&& \3n\3n\3n\quad  + {\mathbb{E}} \int_t^T\big\langle
P(\tau)C(\tau)x_{1}(\tau),
v_{2}(\tau)\big\rangle_{H}d\tau + {\mathbb{E}}
\int_t^T \big\langle  P(\tau)v_{1}(\tau), C(\tau)x_{2}(\tau)+v_{2}(\tau)\big\rangle_{H}d\tau\nonumber\\
&& \3n\3n\3n\quad + {\mathbb{E}} \int_t^T
\big\langle v_{1}(\tau),
\Lambda(\tau)x_2(\tau)\big\rangle_{H_\lambda,
H_\lambda'}d\tau+ {\mathbb{E}} \int_t^T \big\langle
\Lambda(\tau)x_1(\tau), v_{2}(\tau)
\big\rangle_{H_\lambda',H_\lambda}d\tau,\nonumber
\end{eqnarray}
 
where $x_1(\cdot)$ and $x_2(\cdot)$ solve
\eqref{op-fsystem1} and \eqref{op-fsystem2},
respectively.

title: Remark
body_md:
It is more natural to require the optimal
feedback operator $\Theta(\cdot)\in \Upsilon_2(H;U)$
other than $\Theta(\cdot)\in \Upsilon_2(H;U)\cap
\Upsilon_2(H_\lambda;\widetilde U)$.  Nevertheless, we do
not know how to prove Theorem \ref{5.7-th1} with
such condition now.
head: environment

label: 5.7-th1-2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{5.7-th1-2}
Let  {\bf (AS1)}-- {\bf (AS4)} hold and $A$
generates a $C_0$-semigroup on $H$. Then,
Problem (SLQ) admits a unique optimal feedback
operator $\Theta(\cdot)\in \widetilde\Upsilon_2(H,U)\cap
\widetilde\Upsilon_2(H_\lambda;\widetilde U)$ if and only if the
Riccati equation \eqref{5.5-eq6} has a unique
transposition solution
$\big(P(\cdot),\Lambda(\cdot)\big)\in C_{{\mathbb{F}},w}([0,T];
L^{\infty}(\Omega;{\cal S}(H))) \times
L^2_{{\mathbb{F}},D,w}(0,T; {\cal S}(H))$ such that
 
$$\begin{array}{ll}
 
\noalign{\smallskip} \displaystyle K(\cdot)^{-1}\big[B(\cdot)^* P(\cdot)
+D(\cdot)^* P(\cdot)C(\cdot) +
D(\cdot)^*\Lambda(\cdot)\big]\in
\widetilde\Upsilon_2(H;U)\cap
\widetilde\Upsilon_2(H_\lambda;\widetilde
U).
 
\end{array}
$$
 
In this case, the optimal feedback operator $\Theta(\cdot)$ is given by
 
$$\begin{array}{ll}
 
\noalign{\smallskip} \displaystyle \Theta(\cdot)=-K(\cdot)^{-1}[B(\cdot)^* P(\cdot)
+D(\cdot)^* P(\cdot)C(\cdot) + D(\cdot)^*\Lambda(\cdot)].
 
\end{array}
$$
 
 
Furthermore,\vspace{-4mm}
 
$$\begin{array}{ll}
 
\noalign{\smallskip} \displaystyle
\inf_{u\in
L^2_{\mathbb{F}}(s,T;U)}{\cal J}(s,\eta;u)=\frac{1}{2}\,{\mathbb{E}}\langle
P(s)\eta,\eta\rangle_H.
 
\end{array}
$$
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
At a first glance, it seems that Theorem \ref{5.7-th1-2} is more general than Theorem \ref{5.7-th1}. However, we believe that Theorem \ref{5.7-th1} is more interesting due to the following reasons: first, as we have explained in Remark \ref{3.7-rmk1-1}, {\bf (AS0)} is always fulfilled by controlled SPDEs; second, the space $\Upsilon_2(H;U)\cap \Upsilon_2(H_\lambda;\widetilde
U)$ is larger than the space $\widetilde\Upsilon_2(H;U)\cap
\widetilde\Upsilon_2(H_\lambda;\widetilde
U)$.

label: 3.4-eq31
title: Definition
body_md:
We call $(P(\cdot),\Lambda(\cdot))\in
C_{{\mathbb{F}},w}\big([0,T];L^\infty(\Omega;{\cal L}(H))\big)\times
L^2_{{\mathbb{F}}}\big(0,T;L^2(\Omega;{\mathbb{S}}_2(H;H_\lambda'))\big)$
an $H_\lambda$-transposition solution to the equation
\eqref{Relaxed-t-solution-Riccati} if for any $t\in[0,T]$,   $\tilde
\xi_1,\tilde \xi_2\in L^4_{{\cal F}_t}(\Omega;H)$, $\tilde u_1(\cdot),$
$\tilde u_2(\cdot)\in L^4_{\mathbb{F}}(\Omega;L^2(t,T;H))$ and $\tilde v_1(\cdot),
\tilde v_2(\cdot)$ $\in L^4_{\mathbb{F}}(\Omega;L^2(t,T;H_\lambda))$, it holds that
 
\begin{equation}\label{3.4-eq31}
\begin{array}{ll}
\displaystyle {\mathbb{E}}\big\langle G\tilde x_1(T),\tilde x_2(T)\big\rangle_{H}+ {\mathbb{E}}\int_t^T \big\langle [Q(r)+\Theta(r)^*R(r)\Theta(r)]\tilde x_1(r),\tilde x_2(r)\big\rangle_H dr\\
\noalign{\smallskip} \displaystyle ={\mathbb{E}}\big\langle P(t)\tilde \xi_1,\tilde \xi_2\big\rangle_{H}+{\mathbb{E}}\int_t^T \big\langle P(r)\tilde u_1(r),\tilde x_2(r)\big\rangle_{H} dr+{\mathbb{E}}\int_t^T \big\langle P(r)\tilde x_1(r),\tilde u_2(r)\big\rangle_H dr\\
\noalign{\smallskip} \displaystyle \quad +{\mathbb{E}}\int_t^T \big\langle P(r)C_\Theta(r)\tilde x_1(r),\tilde
v_2(r)\big\rangle _{H} dr+{\mathbb{E}}\int_t^T
\big\langle P(r)\tilde v_1(r), C_\Theta(r)\tilde x_2(r)+\tilde v_2(r)\big\rangle_H dr\\
\noalign{\smallskip} \displaystyle\quad +{\mathbb{E}}\int_t^T \big\langle \tilde v_1(r),\Lambda^*(r) \tilde
x_2(r)\big\rangle_{H_\lambda,H_\lambda'} dr +{\mathbb{E}}\int_t^T \big\langle \tilde
v_2(r),\Lambda(r)\tilde x_1(r)\big\rangle_{H_\lambda,H_\lambda'} dr.
\end{array}
\end{equation}
 
Here $\tilde x_1(\cdot)$ and $\tilde x_2(\cdot)$
solve \eqref{op-fsystem3} and
\eqref{op-fsystem4}, respectively.

body_md:
\label{3.14-lm1}
The equation \eqref{Relaxed-t-solution-Riccati} admits a unique
$H_\lambda$-transposition solution $(P(\cdot),\Lambda(\cdot))$. Moreover,
 
$$
\begin{array}{ll}\displaystyle
|(P(\cdot),\Lambda(\cdot))|_{C_{{\mathbb{F}},w}([0,T];L^\infty(\Omega; {\cal S}(H) ))\times
L^2_{{\mathbb{F}}}(0,T;L^2(\Omega; {\mathbb{S}}_2(H;H_\lambda') ))}\\
\noalign{\smallskip} \displaystyle \leq {\cal C}\big(\big||Q +
\Theta^{*}R\Theta|_{{\cal L}(H)}\big|_{L^\infty_{\mathbb{F}}(\Omega;L^1(0,T))} +

\end{array}
$$

label: lemma5
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma5}
 
For each $t\in[0,T]$, if $u_2=v_2=0$ in the equation
\eqref{op-fsystem4}, then there exists an operator $\Phi(\cdot,t)\in
{\cal L}\big(L^{4}_{{\cal F}_t}(\Omega;H),$ $ L^{4}_{\mathbb{F}}(\Omega;C([t,T];H))\big)$
such that the solution to \eqref{op-fsystem4} can be represented as
$\tilde x_2(\cdot) = \Phi(\cdot,t)\tilde \xi_2$. Further, for any $t\in
[0,T)$, $\xi\in L^{4}_{{\cal F}_t}(\Omega;H)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, there is a $\delta\in
(0,T-t)$ such that for any $s\in [t, t+\delta]$, it holds that
 
\begin{equation}\label{10.31eq1}
|\Phi(\cdot,t)\xi-\Phi(\cdot,s)\xi|_{L^{4}_{\mathbb{F}}(\Omega;C([s,T];H))} <\varepsilon.
\end{equation}

label: Remark-novel-contribution
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Remark-novel-contribution}
 
We point out one essential difference from  the
Markovian study in   \cite[Theorem
3.3]{Wang-COCV-2020}, \cite[Lemma
2.8]{Lu-2020-COCV} due to the appearance of
random coefficients. To this end, let us take a
closer look at (\ref{A-key-contribution}). In
the Markovian setting, the expectation ${\mathbb{E}}$
can be omitted. Then by the separable property
of Hilbert space $H$, $U$ or the Euclidean
space, and the classical Lebesgue's differential
theorem, one can obtain the pointwise limit of
(\ref{A-key-contribution}). This method does not
work in our setting. To overcome this obstacle,
we introduce a proper form of $\xi$ in
\eqref{3.4-eq19}, and suitable Lebesgue's
differential theorem (Lemma
\ref{Lebesgue-differential-theorem}). To the
best of our knowledge, these two technologies
are even new in the counterpart finite
dimensional situation.
